title: SHIELD: Suppressing Hallucinations In LVLM Encoders via Bias and Vulnerability Defense
claim: Model failures stem from three distinct flaws in an upstream component, each shown with a concrete example of how it corrupts the output.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, repeated encoder-LLM pipeline with colored backgrounds
description: Three side-by-side panels with tinted backgrounds (green, yellow, blue) labeled Statistical Bias, Inherent Bias and Vulnerability. Each panel repeats the same mini-pipeline. An input image goes into a peach 'Visual Encoder' box, which produces a 4x4 grid of token squares. The tokens and a handwritten-style 'What's in the image?' prompt feed an 'LLM' box. Below it, a bar chart lists Skier, Cabin, Tree and Car. In the first panel, a ski photo gives some tokens a darker shade and a red-outlined 'Tree' bar. In the second, the input is pure noise, one token is pink, and 'Car' is highlighted in red. In the third, a noisy ski photo gives a corrupted token and a red 'Cabin' bar. The eye goes to the red-highlighted wrong labels and the colored token grids.
caption: Key issues underlying object hallucinations in LVLMs. Statistical bias: the visual encoder overemphasizes frequent visual patterns, distorting fine-grained perception. Inherent bias: the encoder produces erroneous representations of dominant objects in the pretraining data, regardless of input. Vulnerability: the encoder is sensitive to minor perturbations, yielding unreliable features.
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) excel in diverse cross-modal tasks. However, object hallucination, where models produce plausible but inaccurate object descriptions, remains a significant challenge. In contrast to previous work focusing on LLM components, this paper is the first to trace LVLM hallucinations to visual encoders and identifies three key issues: statistical bias, inherent bias, and vulnerability. To address these challenges, we propose SHIELD, a training-free framework that mitigates hallucinations through three strategies: re-weighting visual tokens to reduce statistical bias, introducing noise-derived tokens to counter inherent bias, and applying adversarial attacks with contrastive decoding to address vulnerability. Experiments demonstrate that SHIELD effectively mitigates object hallucinations across diverse benchmarks and LVLM families. Moreover, SHIELD achieves strong performance on the general LVLM benchmark, highlighting its broad applicability. Code is available at https://github.com/hukcc/SHIELD.
